# BeatTheHeat.Asia: the whole map as text

> An interactive systems map of extreme heat in Asia: how heat ripples through 10 systems and 83 consequences, the 21 vicious cycles that make it worse, the 29 actions that could break them, and the 14 kinds of institution that hold those levers. Every claim links to its source.

This is a beta version. BeatTheHeat.Asia is being built by a group of organisations working on extreme heat. It is an independent, work-in-progress project, not an official publication of any one organisation. Listing an organisation does not imply its partnership, affiliation or endorsement. Every claim links to its source; where the evidence is still emerging, the map says so.

Text, data, films and illustrations © BeatTheHeat.Asia contributors, shared under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 (CC BY 4.0, https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/): you may copy, adapt and translate them, with credit and a link to beattheheat.asia. Code is under the MIT licence. Linked sources, quotations, and organisations’ names and logos remain their owners’ and are not covered.

Interactive map: https://beattheheat.asia/ · Generated 2026-10-24

## The web of extreme heat: every consequence, system by system

How extreme heat ripples through 10 systems: 83 consequences and the links between them, each with its evidence.

### Extreme heat: where every cycle starts

Extreme heat is where every cycle on this map starts, and it is no longer only weather. Climate change is already making Asia’s hottest days more frequent.

Summer 2026, June to August:

- 1.5 billion+ people worldwide had at least 30 days of risky heat added by climate change.

- 117 million of them were in India, the most of any country, followed by China (94 million) and Indonesia (83 million).

- 2.8 billion people in Asia, 58% of its population, lived through at least 30 days of risky heat.

A risky heat day is hotter than 90% of the days recorded in that place from 1991 to 2020. Source: Climate Central, Risky heat added by climate change: June to August 2026, https://www.climatecentral.org/climate-matters/risky-summer-heat

### Nature and ecosystems

Heat dries land, burns forests, melts ice and warms the sea, wearing down the ecosystems that feed, water and shelter us.

#### Droughts

Higher temperatures speed up evaporation, so the same rain goes less far and dry spells turn into droughts.

Leads to: Wildfires (Parched land and vegetation burn more easily.); Water shortages (Rivers, wells and reservoirs fall.); Failing harvests (Crops fail without water.); Livestock losses (Less water and fodder for animals.); Wildlife moves into farms and villages (Animals leave parched forests in search of water and food.); City trees and parks die (Trees with no water or root space die in long dry spells.)

#### Wildfires

Hot, dry vegetation ignites more easily and burns longer, sending smoke far beyond the fire itself.

Leads to: Smoke, smog and ozone (Smoke travels hundreds of kilometres from the fire.); Glacier and snow melt (Soot settling on snow and ice darkens it, so it absorbs more sunlight and melts faster.); Extreme heat (Fires release carbon and strip away tree cover that shades and cools the land.)

#### Forest dieback

Heat and drought stress trees until they stop growing, then die, turning forests from shade and carbon stores into fuel.

Leads to: Wildfires (Stressed and dying trees become fuel.); Biodiversity loss (Habitats disappear with the trees.); Wildlife moves into farms and villages (Dying forests offer less food and shelter, pushing animals out.)

#### Drying soils

Heat pulls moisture from the ground when crops and plants need it most.

Leads to: Failing harvests (Moisture vanishes just when crops need it most.); Extreme heat (Dry soil can’t cool itself by evaporation, so more of the sun’s energy becomes heat.)

#### Glacier and snow melt

Mountain glaciers and snowpacks that feed rivers through the dry season are shrinking.

Leads to: Water shortages (Rivers fed by snow and ice run lower in the dry season.); Hydropower falls (Less meltwater reaches the dams.); Extreme heat (Melting snow and ice expose darker ground and water, which absorb more sunlight.)

#### Marine heatwaves and coral bleaching

Ocean heatwaves bleach coral and drive fish away from the waters people depend on.

Leads to: Fisheries decline (Fish move away from warming water, and dying reefs support fewer of them.)

#### Biodiversity loss

Species that can’t move or adapt fast enough decline, weakening pollination, soils and fisheries.

Leads to: Failing harvests (Fewer pollinators and natural pest-eaters mean lower yields.)

#### Wildlife moves into farms and villages

As water and forage dry up, animals leave forests for farms and villages. Crops are raided, people and animals are hurt, hunting for food rises, and closer contact raises the risk of diseases passing from animals to people. In Assam, villagers have grown paddy just for wild elephants, so the herds leave the main harvest alone.

Leads to: Failing harvests (Elephants, wild boar and other animals raid crops.); Infectious diseases spread (Closer contact between people, livestock and wild animals raises the risk of diseases crossing over.); Injuries and accidents rise (Encounters injure and kill people and animals.)

Source: Abrahms et al., Nature Climate Change, 2023: climate change amplifies human–wildlife conflict https://doi.org/10.1038/s41558-023-01608-5

Source: Mongabay India, 2023: Assam farmers grow paddy for wild elephants https://india.mongabay.com/2023/09/video-farmers-grow-paddy-for-wild-elephants-in-assam-to-reduce-conflicts/

Source: Tamil Nadu State Planning Commission, Beating the Heat: Tamil Nadu Heat Mitigation Strategy, 2024 https://spc.tn.gov.in/wp-content/uploads/Heat_Mitigation_Strategy.pdf

### Food and agriculture

Crops, animals, fisheries and the people who work them all have heat limits. Cross them and food gets scarcer and dearer.

#### Failing harvests

Heat during flowering and grain-filling cuts yields of staple crops, even when there is enough rain. Smallholders farming on rain alone, with no irrigation or savings to fall back on, are hit first.

Leads to: Food price spikes (Smaller harvests push up prices.); Farmers fall into debt (A failed season leaves farmers borrowing to eat and to replant.)

#### Livestock losses

Heat-stressed animals eat less, produce less milk and eggs, fall ill and die.

Leads to: Hunger and malnutrition (Less milk, eggs and meat for families who rely on them.)

#### Farmwork hours lost

Farm labourers work in the open sun. In the hottest hours, work becomes dangerous or impossible.

Leads to: Failing harvests (Fields go untended in the hottest hours.); Lost work hours and wages (Farm labourers lose daily wages.)

#### Pests and crop diseases spread

Warmer conditions let many pests and plant diseases breed faster and spread to new areas.

Leads to: Failing harvests (More pests and plant diseases mean more crops lost.)

#### Fisheries decline

As waters warm and reefs die, fish move away or decline, and catches fall. Coastal and riverside families who live from fishing lose food and income together.

Leads to: Hunger and malnutrition (Coastal families lose a vital source of protein and income.)

#### Food spoils faster

Without cool storage, more of every harvest rots between field and plate.

Leads to: Food price spikes (Losses after harvest push up prices.)

#### Food price spikes

Smaller harvests and losses push up prices, felt hardest by families who spend most of their income on food.

Leads to: Hunger and malnutrition (The poorest spend most of their income on food.); Informal workers can’t stop work (Higher prices make it even harder to stop working.)

#### Hunger and malnutrition

When food costs more and incomes fall, families eat less and less well, and children suffer most.

Leads to: Learning suffers in hot classrooms (Hungry children struggle to learn.); Babies and young children at risk (Underfed babies and children have less reserve to survive heat and illness.)

#### Farmers fall into debt

After a failed season, farmers borrow at high interest or sell livestock, land and seed to get by.

Leads to: Failing harvests (Indebted farmers cut back on seed, water and fertiliser, so the next harvest fails more easily.); Forced migration (When debts can’t be repaid, families leave the land to look for work.); Loan repayments slip (Failed harvests leave farm loans unpaid.)

### Water

Heat raises the demand for water just as it shrinks the supply, and lowers its quality.

#### Water shortages

Taps run dry and wells fall just as people, crops and animals need more water to cope with the heat.

Leads to: Longer trips to fetch water (Taps run dry, so someone has to fetch water.); Sanitation and hygiene fail (Without water, sanitation and hygiene fail.); Competition for water (Farms, cities and power plants compete for what is left.); Irrigation demand soars (Dry fields need more irrigation.); Power plants cut output (Power plants need cool water. When rivers run low or warm, they cut output.); City trees and parks die (When water runs short, watering trees and parks is cut first.)

#### Water quality falls

Warm, low water breeds algae and bacteria and concentrates pollution.

Leads to: Infectious diseases spread (Contaminated water spreads disease.)

#### Irrigation demand soars

Hot, dry fields need far more water to keep crops alive.

Leads to: Groundwater over-pumped (Farmers pump harder and deeper to keep crops alive.)

#### Groundwater over-pumped

Farmers and cities pump deeper and harder, draining aquifers faster than rain can refill them.

Leads to: Water shortages (Aquifers fall and wells run dry.)

#### Competition for water

Farms, cities, industry and power plants all compete for a shrinking supply.

Leads to: Conflict over water and land (Scarce water becomes a source of conflict.)

#### Longer trips to fetch water

Where taps fail, someone has to walk further, for longer, in the heat, to bring water home.

Leads to: Care burden falls on women and girls (Fetching water falls mostly on women and girls.); Children pulled out of school (Girls miss school to fetch water.); Violence against women rises (Longer trips for water, often alone, expose women and girls to harassment and assault.)

#### Sanitation and hygiene fail

Without enough water, toilets, handwashing and cleaning suffer.

Leads to: Infectious diseases spread (Poor hygiene spreads diarrhoea and other infections.); Babies and young children at risk (Diarrhoea from unsafe water is most dangerous for the youngest children.)

### Energy

Heat drives up demand for cooling while cutting the ability of power plants and grids to supply it.

#### Cooling demand peaks

As temperatures climb, so does the demand for fans and air conditioning, pushing electricity use to new peaks.

Leads to: Power cuts and grid stress (Peak demand pushes grids to the limit.); Emissions from cooling rise (Most cooling still runs on fossil-fuelled power.); Urban heat islands (Air conditioners pump heat outdoors, warming the streets around them.); Can’t afford to keep cool (Higher bills push poor households into energy poverty.)

#### Power cuts and grid stress

Peak demand and heat-stressed lines and transformers push grids to the edge. Outages switch off cooling when it matters most.

Leads to: Diesel generators run longer (Outages drive those who can afford it to diesel.); Cold chains break (Without power, fridges for food and vaccines fail.); Health systems overwhelmed (Hospitals and clinics lose cooling and equipment when the power fails.); Water shortages (Without power, pumps and treatment plants stop.); Phone and data networks fail (Phone masts and networks fail when the power does.); Small businesses close (Shops and workshops lose power and stock.)

#### Power plants cut output

Coal, gas and nuclear plants need cool water. When rivers run low or warm, they have to produce less.

Leads to: Power cuts and grid stress (Plants cut output just when demand peaks.)

#### Hydropower falls

Low rivers and reservoirs mean less electricity from dams.

Leads to: Power cuts and grid stress (Low reservoirs mean less electricity.)

#### Diesel generators run longer

When the grid fails, homes, shops and hospitals that can afford it switch to diesel.

Leads to: Emissions from cooling rise (Diesel adds still more emissions.); Smoke, smog and ozone (Generators fill streets with fumes.)

#### Emissions from cooling rise

Most cooling still runs on fossil-fuelled power and refrigerants that warm the planet.

Leads to: Extreme heat (Emissions add to the warming that drives demand for cooling.)

#### Can’t afford to keep cool

For the poorest households, fans, cooling and electricity bills are out of reach.

Leads to: Heatstroke and heat exhaustion (With no way to cool down at home, heat builds up in the body.)

#### Cold chains break

Without reliable power, fridges for food, medicines and vaccines fail.

Leads to: Food spoils faster (Food rots without refrigeration.); Infectious diseases spread (Spoiled vaccines leave people unprotected.)

### Cities and infrastructure

Concrete, crowding and ageing infrastructure turn cities into amplifiers of heat.

#### Urban heat islands

Dense surfaces, little shade and waste heat keep city cores several degrees hotter than their surroundings, especially at night. This is the urban heat island effect.

Leads to: Cooling demand peaks (A hotter city needs even more cooling.); Sleepless hot nights (Cities hold their heat overnight.); City trees and parks die (Hotter streets stress trees further; many city species are already past their heat limits.)

#### Homes that trap heat

Tin roofs, poor ventilation and crowded rooms can make homes hotter inside than out, leaving nowhere safe to rest.

Leads to: Heatstroke and heat exhaustion (With no cool place to recover, heat builds up day after day.); Deepening inequality (Hot homes cost sleep, health and earnings, so the gap widens.); Sleepless hot nights (Rooms stay hot all night.)

#### Roads, rails and runways strained

Rails buckle, roads soften and hot, thin air means planes need longer runways or must carry less.

Leads to: Transport disrupted (Buckled rails and softened roads slow everything down.); Public budgets strained (Repairs drain public budgets.)

#### Transport disrupted

Speed limits, cancellations and breakdowns slow the movement of people and goods.

Leads to: Supply chains disrupted (Goods stop moving.)

#### Smoke, smog and ozone

Heat speeds up the chemistry that forms ground-level ozone, and still, hot air traps pollution and smoke.

Leads to: Breathing problems worsen (Ozone and smoke inflame the lungs.)

#### Streets and parks unusable

Markets, streets and parks become too hot to use in the middle of the day.

Leads to: Small businesses close (Street trade and markets empty out.); Older people isolated at home (People stay indoors and alone.); Customers stay home (When streets are too hot to walk, shoppers stay away.)

#### City trees and parks die

Heat, drought and missing upkeep kill street trees and parks just when their shade is needed. Across 164 cities, 56% of urban tree and shrub species already face temperatures beyond those in their natural range, and in hot cities such as New Delhi and Singapore every species studied is at risk.

Leads to: Urban heat islands (Fewer trees means less shade and less evaporative cooling, so streets heat up.)

Source: Esperon-Rodriguez et al., Nature Climate Change, 2022: climate change increases global risk to urban forests https://www.vibrantcitieslab.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2023/08/climate-change-increases-global-risk-to-urban-forests.pdf

Source: Hansen et al., chapter 10 in Nature-Based Solutions for Cities, 2023: more than 500 of 870 new trees died in a Berlin park https://doi.org/10.4337/9781800376762

#### Green space follows wealth

Trees and parks cluster in better-off neighbourhoods, which can pay for them and for the upkeep that keeps them alive, so poorer districts stay hotter.

Leads to: Urban heat islands (Neighbourhoods with little green run hotter.); Greening pushes people out (When greening finally reaches the least green, cheapest districts as a property upgrade, without protection for tenants, rents rise.)

Source: Wolch, Byrne and Newell, Landscape and Urban Planning, 2014: making cities “just green enough” https://urbansustainability.seas.umich.edu/wp-content/uploads/2014/06/Making-cities-just-green-enough.pdf

Source: Hansen et al., chapter 10 in Nature-Based Solutions for Cities, 2023: tree survival tracks municipal budgets in Santiago https://doi.org/10.4337/9781800376762

#### Phone and data networks fail

Overheating equipment and power cuts take down phone masts, networks and data centres.

Leads to: Emergency services stretched (Warnings and calls for help don’t get through.); Help can’t reach remote places (Without a phone signal, heat warnings never reach the last village.)

### Health

The human body has limits. Heat strains the heart, kidneys, lungs and mind, and the services built to care for them.

#### Heat deaths

Extreme heat kills, often quietly, through failing hearts, kidneys and lungs. Europe’s 2003 heatwave alone is estimated to have caused more than 70,000 deaths.

Leads to: Heat deaths under-recorded (Most heat deaths are recorded as heart, kidney or lung failure.); Deepening inequality (Families lose breadwinners and carers.)

#### Heatstroke and heat exhaustion

When the body can no longer cool itself, heat exhaustion can tip into heatstroke: a medical emergency that can kill. India’s suspected heatstroke cases rose more than tenfold in two summers, from 4,481 in 2022 to over 48,000 in 2024. Humid heat is the most dangerous: when the wet-bulb temperature is high, sweat stops cooling the body.

Leads to: Heat deaths (Heatstroke kills if it is not treated quickly.); Health systems overwhelmed (Heat illness brings sudden surges of patients.); Lost work hours and wages (Illness means days off work, and for daily earners no work means no pay.); Medical costs and debt (Treatment and lost days are paid for out of pocket.)

#### Kidney and heart strain

Sweating and dehydration make the heart work harder and can damage the kidneys, especially with repeated exposure.

Leads to: Heat deaths (Many heat deaths are heart and kidney failures.)

#### Breathing problems worsen

Ozone, smoke and hot air inflame airways and worsen asthma and lung disease.

Leads to: Heat deaths (Breathing problems turn fatal in the heat.)

#### Risks in pregnancy

Each 1 °C rise in temperature raises the odds of preterm birth by about 5%, and a heatwave by about 16%. Stillbirths rise too. Women who keep working outdoors or fetching water while pregnant carry the most risk.

Leads to: Health systems overwhelmed (Complications add to the load on maternity care.); Babies and young children at risk (Babies born early or small are more fragile in the heat.)

#### Babies and young children at risk

Babies and small children overheat and dehydrate faster than adults, and can’t say when they are struggling. Heat brings more diarrhoea, malnutrition and hospital visits for the youngest.

Leads to: Care burden falls on women and girls (Sick babies and children need someone at home to look after them, usually their mother.)

#### Mental health suffers

Heat is linked to more anxiety, distress and suicide, and to worse outcomes for people living with mental illness.

Leads to: Sleepless hot nights (Stress and anxiety make sleep even harder.); Violence and crime rise (Frayed tempers spill over into violence.)

#### Sleepless hot nights

When nights stay hot, the body never recovers from the day, so the next day starts already depleted.

Leads to: Mental health suffers (Poor sleep wears down mood and the ability to cope.); Heatstroke and heat exhaustion (Without cool nights, the body starts each day already overheated.)

#### Infectious diseases spread

Warmth helps mosquitoes that carry dengue thrive, and dirty water and spoiled food spread illness.

Leads to: Health systems overwhelmed (Outbreaks add to the caseload.)

#### Injuries and accidents rise

Heat dulls concentration and coordination, so accidents at work, on the road and at home increase.

Leads to: Health systems overwhelmed (More casualties to treat.); Lost work hours and wages (Injured workers lose income.)

#### Health systems overwhelmed

Heatwaves bring surges of patients just as staff, power and supplies are under strain.

Leads to: Heatstroke and heat exhaustion (Overstretched services treat people later, and heat illness turns severe fast.)

### Work and economy

Heat slows hands, closes businesses and squeezes the incomes of those with the least margin.

#### Lost work hours and wages

The International Labour Organization projects that heat stress could cut 2.2% of all working hours worldwide by 2030, the equivalent of 80 million full-time jobs.

Leads to: Informal workers can’t stop work (Lost income leaves even less margin, so the next heatwave has to be worked through too.); Deepening inequality (Lost earnings hurt most where there are no savings to fall back on.); Hunger and malnutrition (Less income means less food.); Violence against women rises (Lost income and stress at home raise the risk of violence against women.); Loan repayments slip (Lost wages make household and microfinance repayments harder.)

#### Informal workers can’t stop work

Without paid leave, contracts or savings, stopping work means losing the day’s income. So people keep working through dangerous heat. About three in four Indian workers, some 380 million people, depend on heat-exposed work.

Leads to: Heatstroke and heat exhaustion (Working through the hottest hours without shade, water or rest raises the risk of heat illness.); Injuries and accidents rise (Fatigue and heat cause accidents.); Care burden falls on women and girls (When workers fall ill, someone has to care for them, usually women.)

#### Productivity falls

Above a certain temperature, people work more slowly and make more mistakes, indoors and out. Across 2.7 million firms in 23 advanced economies, ten extra days above 35 °C cut a year’s labour productivity by 0.3%, and days above 40 °C did five times the damage. In humid, still air the loss roughly doubles.

Leads to: Lost work hours and wages (Slower work means lower output and pay.); Public budgets strained (Lower output means lower tax revenue.)

#### Medical costs and debt

Treatment, medicines and lost days are often paid for out of pocket, pushing households into debt.

Leads to: Informal workers can’t stop work (Debt repayments remove any option to stop work in the heat.); Can’t afford to keep cool (Debt leaves nothing for electricity or cooling.)

#### Small businesses close

Street vendors, workshops and shops lose customers, stock and power, and many shut for good.

Leads to: Lost work hours and wages (Closed businesses mean lost jobs.); Deepening inequality (Small firms lose the most in hot years while the largest firms gain, so heat widens the gap between them.); Loan repayments slip (Lost sales leave small firms short of cash to repay their loans.)

#### Supply chains disrupted

Heat slows factories, ports, roads and warehouses. The delays ripple through prices and jobs far away.

Leads to: Food price spikes (Delays and losses push up prices.)

#### Customers stay home

Heat empties markets and high streets in the hottest hours. Spending shifts to cooled malls and cooling products, while street vendors, small shops, restaurants and hotels lose sales.

Leads to: Small businesses close (Fewer customers mean lost sales and spoiled stock.)

#### Tourism shifts away

Visitors avoid places and seasons that become too hot, taking jobs and income with them.

Leads to: Lost work hours and wages (Fewer visitors, fewer jobs.)

### Education

Hot classrooms and closed schools cost children learning that shows up years later as lower skills and earnings.

#### Schools close in heatwaves

When classrooms become dangerous, schools shut, sometimes for weeks.

Leads to: Learning suffers in hot classrooms (Lost school days mean lost learning.); Care burden falls on women and girls (Children at home need someone to look after them.); Hunger and malnutrition (Children who rely on school meals go without them when schools shut.)

#### Learning suffers in hot classrooms

Studies link hotter school days to measurably lower learning and exam results.

Leads to: Lower skills and earnings (Lost learning becomes lower earnings later.)

#### Children pulled out of school

When families are squeezed, children, often girls, leave school to work, care or fetch water.

Leads to: Lower skills and earnings (Leaving school early limits a whole life’s options.)

#### Lower skills and earnings

Learning lost today becomes lower skills and lower earnings for a lifetime.

Leads to: Deepening inequality (Gaps in learning become gaps in income.)

### Society and security

Heat frays the social fabric: it isolates, displaces, divides and widens every existing gap.

#### Deepening inequality

Every impact lands hardest on those with the least protection, widening gaps in health, income and opportunity.

Leads to: Green space follows wealth (Better-off districts can pay for trees and parks, and for the upkeep that keeps them alive.); Children pulled out of school (Poorer households pull children out of school to work, care or fetch water.); Forced migration (When the gap becomes unbearable, people move.)

#### Care burden falls on women and girls

When people fall ill, schools close or water runs short, the extra caring and fetching usually falls on women and girls. In India, women already lose about 19% of their paid working hours to heat.

Leads to: Deepening inequality (Unpaid care pulls women and girls out of paid work and school.)

#### Older people isolated at home

Older people living alone are among the most likely to die in a heatwave. Many victims of Chicago’s 1995 heatwave died alone at home.

Leads to: Heat deaths (Older people alone at home are among the most likely to die.)

#### Violence and crime rise

Hot days are linked to more aggression, domestic violence and violent crime.

Leads to: Social trust frays (Violence erodes trust.)

#### Violence against women rises

Across India, Nepal and Pakistan, each 1 °C rise in yearly temperature was linked to about 4.5% more violence by husbands and partners. Lost income, stress and crowded hot homes all play a part.

Leads to: Mental health suffers (Violence leaves lasting harm to mental health.); Deepening inequality (Violence keeps women out of work, decisions and public life.)

#### Conflict over water and land

Where water and pasture shrink, disputes between communities can turn violent.

Leads to: Forced migration (Conflict forces people from their homes.)

#### Greening pushes people out

New parks and greening can raise rents and land prices until the poorer residents they were meant to cool are pushed out, often into hotter, more crowded housing. This is green gentrification. Across 28 North American and European cities, greening in the 1990s and 2000s was followed by gentrification in 17.

Leads to: Homes that trap heat (People pushed out often land in hotter, more crowded housing.)

Source: Anguelovski et al., Nature Communications, 2022: green gentrification in European and North American cities https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-022-31572-1

Source: Bangkok: a master’s thesis on Pathumwananurak Park, built where the Rong Poon community lived https://www.researchgate.net/publication/369538102_Green_Gentrification_and_The_Value_of_Urban_Nature_Case_Study_of_Pathumwananurak_Park_Bangkok

#### Forced migration

When land, work and water fail, families may be forced to move, often into cities that are hotter still.

Leads to: Homes that trap heat (People forced to move often end up in crowded, poorly built housing that traps heat.); Violence against women rises (Displaced women and girls face higher risks of violence and exploitation.)

#### Mass gatherings turn deadly

Crowds in open sun with little shade or water are deadly. During the 2024 Hajj, more than 1,300 pilgrims died in extreme heat.

Leads to: Heat deaths (Crowds in the open sun turn deadly.); Emergency services stretched (Mass casualties overwhelm responders.)

#### Social trust frays

Violence, unequal suffering and failing services erode trust between neighbours and in institutions.

Leads to: Older people isolated at home (Weaker community ties leave more people alone.)

### Governance and finance

The institutions that decide who is protected, and who pays, are themselves strained by heat.

#### Emergency services stretched

Ambulances, fire crews and emergency rooms are swamped all at once.

Leads to: Heat deaths (When responders are stretched, help arrives too late.); Public budgets strained (Reacting after the fact costs far more than preparing.)

#### Public budgets strained

Repairs, emergency response, lost tax revenue and relief payments all drain public money.

Leads to: Heat protection underfunded (Stretched budgets leave little for heat protection.)

#### Insurance losses and retreat

Rising losses push premiums up and insurers out, leaving more people and businesses unprotected.

Leads to: Public budgets strained (When insurers retreat, governments carry the losses.); Small businesses close (Uninsured losses close small businesses.)

#### Heat deaths under-recorded

Heat is rarely written on death certificates. Most heat deaths are recorded as heart, kidney or lung failure.

Leads to: Heat protection underfunded (What isn’t counted isn’t funded.)

#### Heat protection underfunded

Warnings, cooling centres, outreach and heat-ready services get a small share of budgets compared with floods or storms.

Leads to: Heat deaths (Without warnings, cooling centres and outreach, more people die.); Emergency services stretched (Without prevention, emergencies multiply.); Health systems overwhelmed (Clinics aren’t prepared for heat.); Insurance losses and retreat (Unmanaged risk drives insurers away.)

#### Help can’t reach remote places

In remote villages, islands, hills and river settlements, the nearest clinic, cool shelter or reliable power can be hours away, and heat warnings often never arrive.

Leads to: Heat deaths (When help is hours away, treatable heat illness turns fatal.); Heat deaths under-recorded (Deaths far from clinics are rarely recorded as heat deaths.)

#### Loan repayments slip

When heat cuts sales, harvests or wages, small firms and households fall behind on loans, and lenders collect less.

Leads to: Borrowing costs rise (Lenders respond to missed repayments by charging more, asking for more collateral and lending less.)

#### Borrowing costs rise

Lenders and rating agencies increasingly price climate risk into borrowing. After heat shocks, banks have charged small firms more, asked for more collateral and lent less.

Leads to: Public budgets strained (Higher borrowing costs leave less to spend.); Small businesses close (Dearer, scarcer credit leaves small firms unable to restock, cool their premises or ride out the next heatwave.)

#### Elections and public services disrupted

Heat disrupts voting, courts and public offices. Polling staff died in heatwaves during India’s 2024 general election.

Leads to: Social trust frays (Disrupted elections and services test public trust.)

## Vicious cycles of extreme heat, and where they can be broken

21 vicious cycles in which extreme heat feeds itself, traps people or overwhelms institutions, with where each one plays out in Asia, the evidence, and the actions that could break it.

### Loops that feed the heat itself

#### The global cooling loop

Cooling powered by fossil fuels adds to the warming that makes us need more cooling.

The cycle: Extreme heat → Energy → Cooling demand peaks → Emissions from cooling rise → back to the start.

Where it plays out: Fast-growing cities across South and Southeast Asia, where air-conditioner ownership is rising quickly.

Where it breaks: Clean, efficient cooling

- The world’s stock of air conditioners is set to grow from 1.6 billion to 5.6 billion by 2050, and the energy they use to triple, unless efficiency improves. (International Energy Agency, 2018, https://www.iea.org/reports/the-future-of-cooling)

#### The dry-soil loop

Heat dries the soil. Dry soil can’t cool itself, so the land heats up faster.

The cycle: Extreme heat → Nature and ecosystems → Drying soils → back to the start.

Where it plays out: Rain-fed farmland on the Indian subcontinent and in mainland Southeast Asia during the hot, dry pre-monsoon months.

Where it breaks: Deep emission cuts, Keep water in the soil

- Reviews the evidence that dry soils amplify hot temperatures: with less water to evaporate, more of the sun’s energy goes into heating the air. (Seneviratne et al., Earth-Science Reviews, 2010, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.earscirev.2010.02.004)

#### The melting-ice loop

Heat melts ice. Darker ground and water absorb more sunlight, and the melting speeds up.

The cycle: Extreme heat → Nature and ecosystems → Glacier and snow melt → back to the start.

Where it plays out: The Hindu Kush Himalaya, whose snow and ice feed rivers such as the Indus, Ganges and Brahmaputra.

Where it breaks: Deep emission cuts, Cut black carbon

- Glaciers lost ice 65% faster in the 2010s than in the decade before. At 1.5–2 °C of warming, glaciers across the region lose 30–50% of their volume by 2100. (ICIMOD, 2023, https://lib.icimod.org/record/36322)

#### The wildfire loop

Heat dries forests into fuel. Fires release carbon and strip away the trees that cool the land.

The cycle: Extreme heat → Nature and ecosystems → Wildfires → back to the start.

Where it plays out: The dry-season burning belt of northern Thailand, Myanmar and Laos, and Indonesia’s peatlands.

Where it breaks: Deep emission cuts, Fire-smart landscapes

- Climate change and land-use change are making wildfires worse. Extreme fires are projected to rise by up to 14% by 2030 and 50% by the end of the century. (UNEP and GRID-Arendal, 2022, https://www.unep.org/resources/report/spreading-wildfire-rising-threat-extraordinary-landscape-fires)

### Loops that break the systems we rely on

#### The cooling trap

Air conditioning heats the street, and a hotter city needs even more air conditioning.

The cycle: Cooling demand peaks → Urban heat islands → back to the start.

Where it plays out: Dense, high-rise city cores such as Hong Kong, Bangkok and Metro Manila.

Where it breaks: Cool by design, Green, cool cities

- In a Phoenix heatwave, waste heat from air conditioners raised night-time air temperatures by more than 1 °C in parts of the city. (Salamanca et al., Journal of Geophysical Research, 2014 (summary by Arizona State University), https://news.asu.edu/content/excess-heat-air-conditioners-causes-higher-nighttime-temperatures)

- China, India and Indonesia are expected to account for half of the world’s air conditioners by 2050. (International Energy Agency, 2018, https://www.iea.org/reports/the-future-of-cooling)

- Chennai’s built-up area more than doubled between 2000 and 2020, and night-time land surface temperatures in its urban areas run about 2 °C higher than on its peri-urban edges. (Tamil Nadu State Planning Commission, 2024, https://spc.tn.gov.in/wp-content/uploads/Heat_Mitigation_Strategy.pdf)

- Singapore’s commercial centre has measured up to about 7 °C warmer than its outskirts on calm, clear nights. (Cooling Singapore, citing Chow and Roth, 2006, https://www.thegpsc.org/sites/gpsc/files/cooling_singapore_-_digital_urban_climate_twin.pdf)

#### The energy–water loop

Water systems need power and power plants need water. In a heatwave, each failure deepens the other.

The cycle: Power cuts and grid stress → Water shortages → Power plants cut output → back to the start.

Where it plays out: Coal-fired power plants along water-stressed rivers in India.

Where it breaks: Power that doesn’t need water, Backup power for water

- 14 of India’s 20 largest thermal utilities shut down at least once for lack of water between 2013 and 2016. Water shortages cost 14 TWh of power in 2016. (World Resources Institute, 2018, https://www.wri.org/insights/40-indias-thermal-power-plants-are-water-scarce-areas-threatening-shutdowns)

#### The groundwater loop

Dry fields need more water, so farmers pump harder, aquifers fall and the shortage deepens.

The cycle: Water shortages → Irrigation demand soars → Groundwater over-pumped → back to the start.

Where it plays out: Punjab and Haryana in northwest India, where groundwater tables have been falling for decades.

Where it breaks: Smart irrigation and groundwater rules

- Satellites show Rajasthan, Punjab and Haryana lost 109 km³ of groundwater between 2002 and 2008, mainly to irrigation, while rainfall stayed close to normal. (Rodell, Velicogna and Famiglietti, Nature, 2009, https://www.nature.com/articles/nature08238)

#### The dying-green loop

Heat and drought kill city trees. Without their shade the streets get hotter, and hotter streets kill more trees.

The cycle: City trees and parks die → Urban heat islands → back to the start.

Where it plays out: Hot, fast-growing cities such as New Delhi and Singapore, where every urban tree species studied is at risk from rising heat.

Where it breaks: Keep city trees alive

- Of 3,129 tree and shrub species in 164 cities, 56% already face temperatures beyond those in their natural range, rising to about 76% by 2050 under a mid-range warming scenario. Risk is highest in low-latitude cities such as New Delhi and Singapore. (Esperon-Rodriguez et al., Nature Climate Change, 2022, https://www.vibrantcitieslab.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2023/08/climate-change-increases-global-risk-to-urban-forests.pdf)

- Drought stops urban trees from cooling through transpiration. In one Berlin park more than 500 of 870 new trees died within ten years despite watering, and Berlin cut about 44,000 street trees between 2012 and 2019 while planting about 18,000. (Hansen et al., chapter 10 in Nature-Based Solutions for Cities, 2023, https://doi.org/10.4337/9781800376762)

- Tree shade sharply lowers the radiant heat people feel by day, which is the cooling lost when trees die. (Middel et al., Bulletin of the American Meteorological Society, https://par.nsf.gov/biblio/10230332-grades-shade)

#### The overwhelmed-clinic loop

Heat illness floods clinics. Overwhelmed clinics treat people later, and more cases become severe.

The cycle: Heatstroke and heat exhaustion → Health systems overwhelmed → back to the start.

Where it plays out: District and city hospitals during South Asia’s pre-monsoon heatwaves.

Where it breaks: Heat action plans, Heat-ready health services

- Heat-related deaths among people over 65 reached a record 167% above the 1990s level in 2023. (Lancet Countdown, The Lancet, 2024, https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(24)01822-1)

- After Ahmedabad’s heat action plan prepared hospitals and warned the public, an estimated 1,190 deaths a year were avoided. (Hess et al., Journal of Environmental and Public Health, 2018, https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6236972/)

### Loops that trap people

#### The poverty–heat trap

People who can’t afford to stop working fall ill. Illness costs income, and lost income makes stopping even less affordable.

The cycle: Informal workers can’t stop work → Heatstroke and heat exhaustion → Lost work hours and wages → back to the start.

Where it plays out: Construction sites, brick kilns, farms and street markets across South and Southeast Asia.

Where it breaks: Heat-safe work, Income protection in heatwaves, Social protection floors

- Across 2.7 million firms in 23 advanced economies, including Japan and Korea, ten extra days above 35 °C cut yearly labour productivity by 0.3%, and over 1.5% above 40 °C. Very humid places lost 0.75%, more than double the average. Korea has already lost about 0.15% of productivity to added heat since the early 2000s. (OECD Economics Department, Working Paper No. 1828, 2024, https://doi.org/10.1787/19d94638-en)

- Up to three-quarters of India’s workforce, about 380 million people, depend on heat-exposed labour, work that produces nearly half of the country’s GDP. (World Bank, 2022, reported by Down To Earth, https://www.downtoearth.org.in/climate-change/heatwaves-in-india-could-soon-break-human-survivability-limit-says-world-bank-analysis-86431)

- Heat stress is projected to cost 2.2% of all working hours by 2030, equal to 80 million full-time jobs. South Asia is among the worst hit, losing about 5% of working hours. (International Labour Organization, 2019, https://www.ilo.org/resource/news/increase-heat-stress-predicted-bring-productivity-loss-equivalent-80)

- Heat exposure put a record 512 billion potential labour hours at risk in 2023, with potential income losses of US$835 billion. (Lancet Countdown, The Lancet, 2024, https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(24)01822-1)

- Heat-related illness cost Bangladesh 250 million workdays in 2024, worth up to US$1.78 billion, about 0.4% of GDP. Since 1980 the ‘feels-like’ temperature has risen by 4.5 °C. (World Bank, 2025, https://www.worldbank.org/en/news/press-release/2025/09/16/bangladesh-faces-health-and-economic-risks-from-rising-temperature-world-bank)

#### The medical-debt trap

Treatment costs push families into debt. Debt removes any option to rest, and working through the heat brings more illness.

The cycle: Heatstroke and heat exhaustion → Medical costs and debt → Informal workers can’t stop work → back to the start.

Where it plays out: Households without health insurance, where most medical costs are paid out of pocket.

Where it breaks: Heat-safe work, Free care for heat illness

- Medicine costs alone were catastrophic for 11.2% of Indian households in 2011–12, about 29 million households. (Selvaraj, Farooqui and Karan, BMJ Open, 2018, https://bmjopen.bmj.com/content/8/5/e018020)

- In a survey of more than 2,000 residents of five cities, heat harmed health, cut incomes and working hours, and pushed some households towards high-interest loans. Women and people with disabilities faced the hardest trade-offs between health, work and care. (American Red Cross, Red Cross Red Crescent Climate Centre, Nepal Red Cross Society and Bangladesh Red Crescent Society, 2026, https://www.climatecentre.org/publications/17312/the-lived-experiences-of-vulnerable-populations-in-the-context-of-extreme-heat-a-comprehensive-narrative-report-based-on-survey-data-from-five-cities-in-nepal-and-bangladesh/)

#### The energy-poverty trap

People who can’t afford to cool fall ill. Illness brings debt, and debt puts cooling even further out of reach.

The cycle: Can’t afford to keep cool → Heatstroke and heat exhaustion → Medical costs and debt → back to the start.

Where it plays out: Tin-roofed informal settlements in cities such as Dhaka, Karachi and Mumbai.

Where it breaks: Free care for heat illness, Affordable cooling for the poorest

- 1.12 billion of the rural and urban poor are at high risk because they lack access to cooling. (Sustainable Energy for All, 2023, https://www.seforall.org/our-work/research-analysis/chilling-prospects-series/chilling-prospects-global-access-to-cooling-gaps-2023)

#### The displacement loop

People forced to move often land in heat-trapping housing, fall ill, lose income, fall further behind, and are forced to move again.

The cycle: Forced migration → Homes that trap heat → Heatstroke and heat exhaustion → Lost work hours and wages → Deepening inequality → back to the start.

Where it plays out: Migrant settlements on the edges of fast-growing cities such as Dhaka.

Where it breaks: Income protection in heatwaves, Cool, affordable housing

- Without action, climate change could force up to 216 million people to move within their own countries by 2050, including about 40 million in South Asia. (World Bank, 2021, https://openknowledge.worldbank.org/handle/10986/36248)

#### The lost-schooling loop

Children pulled out of school earn less as adults, and poorer families pull more children out of school.

The cycle: Children pulled out of school → Lower skills and earnings → Deepening inequality → back to the start.

Where it plays out: School systems that closed classrooms during the 2024 heatwaves, including in the Philippines and Bangladesh.

Where it breaks: Keep children in school

- Without air conditioning, each 1 °F hotter school year cuts that year’s learning by about 1%, and the losses fall hardest on disadvantaged students. (Park, Goodman, Hurwitz and Smith, American Economic Journal: Economic Policy, 2020, https://www.aeaweb.org/doi/10.1257/pol.20180612)

- Heatwaves disrupted schooling for an estimated 171 million students in 2024. South Asia was the most affected region. (UNICEF, 2025, https://www.unicef.org/reports/learning-interrupted-global-snapshot-2024)

- In early April 2024, 5,288 schools across the Philippines switched to remote learning as the heat index reached danger levels, affecting more than 3.6 million students. (AFP via Malay Mail, April 2024, https://www.malaymail.com/news/world/2024/04/05/thousands-of-philippine-schools-suspend-in-person-classes-due-to-heat-says-education-dept/127511)

- Bangladesh closed schools for about 33 million children in its April 2024 heatwave, and Cambodia cut the school day by two hours. (NBC News, 2024, https://www.nbcnews.com/news/world/schools-close-extreme-heat-philippines-bangladesh-asia-rcna149485)

#### The sleepless-nights loop

Hot nights wreck sleep. Poor sleep frays mental health, and stress makes sleep harder still.

The cycle: Sleepless hot nights → Mental health suffers → back to the start.

Where it plays out: Tropical cities whose nights stay hot, such as Bangkok, Chennai and Ho Chi Minh City.

Where it breaks: Cool nights and support

- Data from 47,628 people in 68 countries shows hot nights shorten sleep, with bigger losses for older people and in lower-income countries. (Minor et al., One Earth, 2022, https://orbit.dtu.dk/en/publications/rising-temperatures-erode-human-sleep-globally/)

- A review of 114 studies links higher temperatures with poorer mental health, including higher suicide rates. (Thompson et al., The Lancet Planetary Health, 2023 (summary by Imperial College London), https://www.imperial.ac.uk/news/246058/rising-temperatures-associated-with-poorer-mental/)

- Over the last decade, nearly 70% of India’s districts gained five or more very warm nights each summer, while only about 28% saw a similar rise in very hot days. Mumbai gained 15 very warm nights a summer, and Bengaluru 11. (Council on Energy, Environment and Water (CEEW), 2025, https://www.ceew.in/sites/default/files/ceew-how-extreme-heat-is-impacting-india-final-web-file.pdf)

- Tamil Nadu’s summer minimum temperatures have risen by about 0.75 °C since the 1980s, and about 56% of its people now live where summer nights are warmer than the 1981–2011 average. (Tamil Nadu State Planning Commission, 2024, https://spc.tn.gov.in/wp-content/uploads/Heat_Mitigation_Strategy.pdf)

#### The green-displacement loop

Green space follows wealth. When greening reaches poorer districts without protection, rents rise, residents are pushed into hotter housing, and the gap grows.

The cycle: Deepening inequality → Green space follows wealth → Greening pushes people out → Homes that trap heat → back to the start.

Where it plays out: Riverbanks, canals and old inner-city sites turned into parks, as studied in Bangkok and Seoul.

Where it breaks: Green without pushing people out

- Across 28 cities in 9 countries, greening in the 1990s and 2000s was strongly linked to gentrification between 2000 and 2016 in 17 of them. (Anguelovski et al., Nature Communications, 2022, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-022-31572-1)

- Green space tends to favour wealthier neighbourhoods, and new parks meant to fix that can raise housing costs and displace the residents they were meant to help. Small, local projects are more likely to reach those who need them. (Wolch, Byrne and Newell, Landscape and Urban Planning, 2014, https://urbansustainability.seas.umich.edu/wp-content/uploads/2014/06/Making-cities-just-green-enough.pdf)

- Fieldwork on how recent gentrification in Bangkok, including green urban renewal, affects the city’s lower-income residents. (Endo, The Developing Economies, 2026, https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/deve.70013)

- Nature-based solutions can deepen injustice when benefits flow to some and costs, including displacement, fall on others; procedural, distributional and recognition justice all need attention. (Chapter 3 in Nature-Based Solutions for Cities, 2023, https://doi.org/10.4337/9781800376762)

#### The heat credit squeeze

Heat empties shops and small firms miss repayments. Banks tighten credit, so firms can’t afford to adapt, and the next heatwave hits harder.

The cycle: Small businesses close → Loan repayments slip → Borrowing costs rise → back to the start.

Where it plays out: Market towns and city high streets in heat-exposed districts, and lenders whose loans are collected door to door, as in microfinance across northern and central India.

Where it breaks: Heat-smart lending

- Across 2.7 million firms in 23 advanced economies, heat cut the productivity of small firms while medium and large firms showed no loss, and the largest grew revenue about 0.6 points faster than small firms after hot years. Losses lasted up to two years. Restaurants and hotels were hit hard, partly through lower demand. (OECD Economics Department, Working Paper No. 1828, 2024, https://doi.org/10.1787/19d94638-en)

- Loan-level bank data from Mexico show that ten extra days of extreme heat in a quarter raise small-business loan delinquency by about 4%, mainly among firms that depend on local customers. Banks then raise rates, ask for more collateral and lend less for two to three quarters. (Aguilar-Gomez et al., summarised in VoxEU, 2024, https://cepr.org/voxeu/columns/heatwaves-ripple-financial-system)

- India’s microfinance industry body said loan quality worsened in April–June 2024, partly because heatwaves cut borrowers’ incomes and lenders’ collections. (Sa-Dhan, reported by Business Standard, 2024, https://www.business-standard.com/finance/news/micro-loan-asset-quality-deteriorates-in-april-june-quarter-sa-dhan-124082700721_1.html)

- A caution for lenders: in Cambodia, researchers found that borrowing to get through climate shocks often delayed the harm rather than removing it, leaving households more indebted for the next shock. (King’s College London, 2023, https://www.kcl.ac.uk/news/new-study-finds-that-microfinance-is-exacerbating-climate-precarity-and-harm-in-cambodia)

- Of 721 Delhi street vendors surveyed in April and May 2024, 80% saw fewer customers during heatwaves and 49% lost income. (Greenpeace India and National Hawkers Federation, 2024, https://www.greenpeace.org/india/en/press/16737/new-report-by-greenpeace-india-and-national-hawkers-federation-reveals-harsh-heatwave-toll-on-street-vendors/)

- Car dealers said heat cut showroom footfall by about 15% in June 2024, leaving them with 62–67 days of unsold stock against a recommended three weeks. A sign of where to look; the link to their loans is not yet measured. (Federation of Automobile Dealers Associations, reported by Orissa Post, 2024, https://www.orissapost.com/passenger-vehicle-retail-sales-dip-7-in-june-as-heatwave-curtails-showroom-visits/amp/)

#### The farm-debt loop

A failed harvest pushes farmers into debt. Debt leaves less for seed, water and fertiliser, so the next harvest fails more easily.

The cycle: Failing harvests → Farmers fall into debt → back to the start.

Where it plays out: Rain-fed farming districts of India, Pakistan and Bangladesh, where a failed season often means borrowing from moneylenders.

Where it breaks: Crop insurance and fair credit

- Heat raises suicide rates in India only during the growing season, when it also cuts crop yields, pointing to farm income losses. The findings have been debated. (Carleton, PNAS, 2017, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5565417/)

- Days above 34 °C make wheat in northern India age early, and crop models may underestimate yield losses at +2 °C by as much as 50%. (Lobell, Sibley and Ortiz-Monasterio, Nature Climate Change, 2012, https://fsi.stanford.edu/node/26622)

- At the International Rice Research Institute’s farm in the Philippines, rice yields fell by about 10% for each 1 °C rise in growing-season night temperature, while daytime highs had little effect. (Peng et al., PNAS, 2004, https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.0403720101)

### Loops inside institutions

#### The invisible-deaths loop

Heat deaths go uncounted, so heat protection goes unfunded, so more people die uncounted.

The cycle: Heat deaths → Heat deaths under-recorded → Heat protection underfunded → back to the start.

Where it plays out: Much of Asia, where death certificates rarely record heat as a cause.

Where it breaks: Count every heat death, Cooling centres and check-ins

- Suspected heatstroke cases rose from 4,481 in 2022 to 48,385 by 28 July 2024, while confirmed heatstroke deaths rose only from 33 to 185. (Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, reply in India’s Rajya Sabha, 6 August 2024, https://rsdebate.nic.in/bitstream/123456789/750681/1/PQ_265_06082024_U1693_p358_p362.pdf)

- In 2020, India’s crime records bureau recorded 530 heatstroke deaths while the disaster agency recorded four. Experts say the low counts weaken preparation. (Associated Press via PBS NewsHour, 2024, https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/india-likely-undercounts-heat-related-deaths-tempering-its-response-officials-say)

- Death certificates usually record only the immediate cause, such as heart failure, so heat as the trigger goes unrecorded. (Down To Earth, 2024, https://www.downtoearth.org.in/climate-change/lost-in-the-heat-the-critical-miscalculation-in-indias-heatwave-mortality-data)

- Between 1 March and 26 July 2026, India’s heat surveillance, covering more than 51,000 reporting units, logged 4,853 heatstroke cases but only 20 heatstroke deaths. (Ministry of Home Affairs, reply in India’s Lok Sabha, reported by Down To Earth, 2026, https://www.downtoearth.org.in/climate-change/india-updates-disaster-list-to-include-heatwaves-and-lightning-after-finance-commission-push)

- Monitors at 24 indoor and outdoor workplaces in Singapore found workers could face more heat stress than nearby national weather stations reported. (NUS Project HeatSafe, 2024, https://medicine.nus.edu.sg/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/PRESS-RELEASE_Project-HeatSafe-18MAR2024-FOR-IMMEDIATE-RELEASE.pdf)

#### The reactive-spending loop

Stretched budgets skimp on prevention. Emergencies multiply, and costly emergency response stretches budgets further.

The cycle: Public budgets strained → Heat protection underfunded → Emergency services stretched → back to the start.

Where it plays out: Disaster budgets designed for floods and cyclones rather than heat.

Where it breaks: Dedicated heat budgets, Anticipatory action

- US$800 million spent on early warning systems in developing countries could avoid US$3–16 billion in losses every year. (Global Commission on Adaptation, 2019, https://openknowledge.worldbank.org/entities/publication/7713887e-5c0c-5fce-9dd0-c18a8875736c)

- Direct response typically gets over half of wildfire spending, while planning and prevention get less than 1%. (UNEP and GRID-Arendal, 2022, https://www.unep.org/resources/report/spreading-wildfire-rising-threat-extraordinary-landscape-fires)

- Of 37 heat action plans reviewed, 11 discussed funding, and 8 of those simply asked departments to find their own money. Only two included a vulnerability assessment. (Centre for Policy Research, 2023, https://cprindia.org/briefsreports/how-is-india-adapting-to-heatwaves-an-assessment-of-heat-action-plans-with-insights-for-transformative-climate-action/)

- In August 2026 India added heatwaves to its notified natural calamities, so national and state disaster response funds can pay for heatwave relief. Before, states could spend only up to 10% of their response fund on locally declared disasters such as heat. Heat mitigation projects are funded separately, from disaster mitigation funds. (Ministry of Home Affairs, reply in India’s Lok Sabha, reported by Down To Earth, 2026, https://www.downtoearth.org.in/climate-change/india-updates-disaster-list-to-include-heatwaves-and-lightning-after-finance-commission-push)

#### The protection-gap loop

As insurers retreat, public budgets absorb the losses, protection is cut, and the risk drives insurers further away.

The cycle: Insurance losses and retreat → Public budgets strained → Heat protection underfunded → back to the start.

Where it plays out: Fast-growing Asian economies where few households or small businesses carry insurance.

Where it breaks: Dedicated heat budgets, Shared risk pools

- Only about 8% of Asia’s US$65 billion in natural catastrophe losses in 2025 was insured. The rest fell on households, businesses and governments. (Swiss Re Institute sigma, reported by Global Reinsurance, https://www.globalreinsurance.com/home/swiss-re-sigma-protection-gap-laid-bare-as-asian-cat-losses-hit-65bn/1458440.article)

## Actions that break the vicious cycles of extreme heat

29 actions that cut a link in one or more vicious cycles of extreme heat: who can take each one, how soon it works, examples from Asia and practical guides.

### Deep emission cuts

Every fraction of a degree avoided weakens every loop that runs through land, ice and forests at once. It also keeps more places within the limits to adaptation, where protecting people still works.

Cuts the link: Extreme heat → Nature and ecosystems. Who can act: National governments, International bodies, Development banks, donors and climate funds.

Could help interrupt: The dry-soil loop, The melting-ice loop, The wildfire loop

In practice: Across 2.7 million firms in 23 advanced economies, places used to heat coped better with days of 30–35 °C, but none had adapted to days above 40 °C. Each degree avoided keeps more days below that line.

- Guide: AR6 Synthesis Report: Climate Change 2023 (Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, 2023) https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/syr/

- Guide: The heat is on: Heat stress, productivity and adaptation among firms (OECD Economics Department, 2024) https://doi.org/10.1787/19d94638-en

### Clean, efficient cooling

Efficient appliances, clean power and low-warming refrigerants break the link between keeping cool and heating the planet.

Cuts the link: Cooling demand peaks → Emissions from cooling rise. Who can act: National governments, Utilities and energy regulators, International bodies.

Could help interrupt: The global cooling loop

In practice: The Kigali Amendment to the Montreal Protocol (2016) commits countries to phase down the most climate-warming refrigerants.

- Guide: India Cooling Action Plan (Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, India, 2019) https://ozonecell.nic.in/home-page/resource-informations/reports-publications/india-cooling-action-plan/

### Keep water in the soil

Mulching, agroforestry, water harvesting and restoring degraded land help soils hold moisture and stay cooler.

Cuts the link: Drying soils → Extreme heat. Who can act: Farmers’ organisations and agriculture agencies, Community and civil society groups, Development banks, donors and climate funds.

Could help interrupt: The dry-soil loop

### Cut black carbon

Cleaner stoves, engines and brick kilns and an end to open burning cut black carbon, the soot that darkens snow and ice.

Cuts the link: Glacier and snow melt → Extreme heat. Who can act: National governments, City and local governments.

Could help interrupt: The melting-ice loop

- Guide: Cleaner brick production: a natural-draught zig-zag kiln case study (Climate and Clean Air Coalition) https://www.ccacoalition.org/resources/cleaner-brick-production-case-study-2-production-bricks-through-natural-draft-zigzag-kiln

### Fire-smart landscapes

Early detection, community fire crews and land management that reduces fuel keep fires small and forests standing.

Cuts the link: Wildfires → Extreme heat. Who can act: National governments, Community and civil society groups.

Could help interrupt: The wildfire loop

- Guide: Spreading like Wildfire: The Rising Threat of Extraordinary Landscape Fires (UNEP and GRID-Arendal, 2022) https://www.unep.org/resources/report/spreading-wildfire-rising-threat-extraordinary-landscape-fires

### Cool by design

Shading, ventilation, reflective roofs and efficient cooling cut the need for air conditioning, and the waste heat it dumps outside.

Cuts the link: Cooling demand peaks → Urban heat islands. Who can act: City and local governments, National governments.

Could help interrupt: The cooling trap

- Guide: Heat in the city: guidance and resources for urban heat (Global Heat Health Information Network (GHHIN)) https://heathealth.info/in-the-city/

### Green, cool cities

Trees, water, cool roofs and cool pavements lower city temperatures and flatten peak demand.

Cuts the link: Urban heat islands → Cooling demand peaks. Who can act: City and local governments, Community and civil society groups.

Could help interrupt: The cooling trap

In practice: Cooling Singapore, a research programme across agencies, models where heat builds up street by street to test which mix of greenery, materials and layout cools each district best. Indian cities and states such as Ahmedabad and Telangana have run programmes that paint roofs to reflect sunlight. The Green Tamil Nadu Mission aims to raise the state’s forest and tree cover from 23.8% to 33% of its land by 2030–31.

- Guide: Urban heat: resources and partner networks (Zurich Climate Resilience Alliance) https://zcralliance.org/resources-urban-heat/

- Guide: Nature-Based Solutions to Climate Change Adaptation in Urban Areas (Kabisch, Korn, Stadler and Bonn (eds), Springer, 2017, open access) https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-56091-5

- Guide: Heat in the city: guidance and resources for urban heat (Global Heat Health Information Network (GHHIN)) https://heathealth.info/in-the-city/

### Keep city trees alive

Water, healthy soil, room for roots, heat-hardy species and a running budget for upkeep keep trees alive through hotter, drier summers, so their shade lasts. Looking after existing trees comes before planting new ones.

Cuts the link: Urban heat islands → City trees and parks die. Who can act: City and local governments, Water authorities, Community and civil society groups.

Could help interrupt: The dying-green loop

In practice: Berlin wrote a shared “good care” manual for its 12 districts, setting maintenance standards for street trees and green spaces, with drought-resistant species for replanting and a calendar of care. It followed losses such as a park where more than 500 of 870 new trees died within ten years despite watering.

- Guide: Climate change increases global risk to urban forests: which city tree species are at risk (Esperon-Rodriguez et al., Nature Climate Change, 2022) https://www.vibrantcitieslab.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2023/08/climate-change-increases-global-risk-to-urban-forests.pdf

### Green without pushing people out

Secure tenure, rent safeguards and designing with residents let poorer neighbourhoods gain shade and parks without losing their homes. Small, local greening that is “just green enough” protects people better than flagship projects.

Cuts the link: Green space follows wealth → Greening pushes people out. Who can act: City and local governments, National governments, Community and civil society groups.

Could help interrupt: The green-displacement loop

In practice: In Bangkok, the Baan Mankong programme of the Community Organizations Development Institute gives canal-side communities subsidies and cheap loans to secure land and rebuild their homes. Along Khlong Lat Phrao, where flood works needed the canal banks, communities planned their own moves and rebuilding instead of being evicted.

- Guide: Urban green space, public health and environmental justice: the challenge of making cities “just green enough” (Wolch, Byrne and Newell, Landscape and Urban Planning, 2014) https://urbansustainability.seas.umich.edu/wp-content/uploads/2014/06/Making-cities-just-green-enough.pdf

- Guide: Greening without gentrification: anti-displacement strategies for parks (Urban Waters Learning Network) https://urbanwaterslearningnetwork.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/Parks-Related-Anti-Displacement-Strategies-report-with-appendix.pdf

### Power that doesn’t need water

Solar and wind use very little water, and dry cooling protects thermal plants when rivers run low or warm.

Cuts the link: Water shortages → Power plants cut output. Who can act: Utilities and energy regulators, National governments.

Could help interrupt: The energy–water loop

### Backup power for water

Solar pumps and backup supply keep water flowing when the grid fails.

Cuts the link: Power cuts and grid stress → Water shortages. Who can act: Water authorities, Utilities and energy regulators.

Could help interrupt: The energy–water loop

- Guide: Climate-resilient water safety plans: managing health risks associated with climate variability and change (World Health Organization, 2017) https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241512794

### Smart irrigation and groundwater rules

Drip irrigation, metering, aquifer recharge and fair pumping rules keep wells from running dry.

Cuts the link: Irrigation demand soars → Groundwater over-pumped. Who can act: Farmers’ organisations and agriculture agencies, Water authorities.

Could help interrupt: The groundwater loop

- Guide: Atal Bhujal Yojana: India’s scheme for community-led groundwater management (Council on Energy, Environment and Water (CEEW)) https://www.ceew.in/publications/atal-bhujal-yojana-scheme-for-sustainable-participatory-groundwater-resources-management

### Crop insurance and fair credit

Crop insurance that pays out after a heat-hit season, affordable credit and heat-tolerant seed stop one bad harvest becoming a debt trap.

Cuts the link: Failing harvests → Farmers fall into debt. Who can act: Banks, insurers and financial regulators, Farmers’ organisations and agriculture agencies, Development banks, donors and climate funds.

Could help interrupt: The farm-debt loop

- Guide: Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana, India’s national crop insurance scheme (Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare, India) https://pmfby.gov.in/

### Heat action plans

Early warnings, public cooling spaces and outreach to the people most at risk prevent illness before it reaches hospital.

Cuts the link: Heatstroke and heat exhaustion → Health systems overwhelmed. Who can act: City and local governments, Health authorities, Weather and climate services.

Could help interrupt: The overwhelmed-clinic loop

In practice: Ahmedabad launched South Asia’s first city heat action plan in 2013; by June 2026, India had more than 250. In Nepal, Dhangadhi, which passes 40 °C every year, published a heat action plan in 2025 with the Nepal Red Cross Society. In Bangladesh, Practical Action is working with communities and local authorities in Khulna to build a heat early warning system that responds to them, where none existed before.

- Guide: Heat action plans and case studies, including Indian cities (Global Heat Health Information Network (GHHIN)) https://heathealth.info/heat-action-plans-and-case-studies/

- Guide: Heat Action Planning Guide for Neighborhoods of Greater Phoenix: planning heat action with residents (The Nature Conservancy and partners, 2019) https://globalfutures.asu.edu/sustainable-cities/wp-content/uploads/sites/17/2023/09/Phoenix-Arizona-Heat-Action-Plan.pdf

- Guide: Heatwaves and health: guidance on warning-system development (WHO and WMO, 2015, in the GHHIN resource library) https://heathealth.info/resources/heatwaves-and-health-guidance-on-warning-system-development/

- Guide: How Extreme Heat is Impacting India: district-level heat risk for all 734 districts, to target plans (Council on Energy, Environment and Water (CEEW), 2025) https://www.ceew.in/sites/default/files/ceew-how-extreme-heat-is-impacting-india-final-web-file.pdf

- Guide: How can heat action plans make Thane a heat-resilient city? (Council on Energy, Environment and Water (CEEW)) https://www.ceew.in/publications/how-can-thane-city-tackle-heatwaves-risks-with-heat-action-plan

### Heat-ready health services

Cooling, backup power, surge plans and trained frontline workers keep clinics working through heatwaves.

Cuts the link: Health systems overwhelmed → Heatstroke and heat exhaustion. Who can act: Health authorities, Development banks, donors and climate funds.

Could help interrupt: The overwhelmed-clinic loop

In practice: On Assam’s Brahmaputra river islands, boat clinics run by C-NES with the National Health Mission switched from diesel to solar power, so lights, fans and vaccine fridges keep working and emergencies can be seen after dark. Tamil Nadu’s heat strategy proposes a simple step for mothers: screen for heat risk in the check-ups of the state’s pregnancy scheme, which has run in various forms since 1987.

- Guide: National Action Plan on Heat-Related Illness (National Centre for Disease Control, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, India, 2021) https://ncdc.mohfw.gov.in/uploads/pdf/heat12.pdf

- Guide: Climate change and health: heat-illness guidelines, emergency cooling guidance and heat stroke units (National Centre for Disease Control, India) https://ncdc.mohfw.gov.in/includes/About/CentresAndDivision/CEOH.php

- Guide: India in a Warming World: Strengthening Heat-Health Action (Council on Energy, Environment and Water (CEEW), for the GHHIN South Asia hub, 2026) https://www.ceew.in/publications/india-heat-health-action

### Heat-safe work

Rest, shade and water during dangerous heat, with paid breaks so that stopping work doesn’t mean losing pay.

Cuts the link: Informal workers can’t stop work → Heatstroke and heat exhaustion. Who can act: National governments, Employers and businesses, Worker organisations and unions.

Could help interrupt: The poverty–heat trap, The medical-debt trap

In practice: Singapore requires hourly wet-bulb globe temperature checks on outdoor worksites and at least 10 minutes’ shaded rest each hour for heavy work at 32 °C or above; in 2024 it inspected 250 workplaces and acted against 78. Several Gulf states ban outdoor work during the hottest midday hours in summer. Since 2023, Spain has required employers to cut or move working hours when the weather agency issues an orange or red heat alert and other measures can’t keep workers safe. Tamil Nadu’s heat strategy proposes building heat protection into the state’s existing occupational safety rules, rather than waiting for a new law.

- Guide: Heat at work: the first joint global guidance on workplace heat stress (WHO and WMO, in the GHHIN resource library) https://heathealth.info/at-work/

### Income protection in heatwaves

Cash that pays out automatically when temperatures cross a danger threshold, so people can afford to stop. Triggers need careful design to limit basis risk: heat that hurts people without triggering a payout.

Cuts the link: Heatstroke and heat exhaustion → Lost work hours and wages. Who can act: Banks, insurers and financial regulators, National governments, Worker organisations and unions.

Could help interrupt: The poverty–heat trap, The displacement loop

In practice: Parametric heat insurance has been piloted with women informal workers in India.

- Guide: Parametric heat and rainfall insurance for informal women workers (VimoSEWA, 2025) https://www.sewainsurance.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/Parametric-Heat-and-Rainfall-Insurance-for-Informal-Women-Workers.pdf

- Guide: Confronting the climate and health nexus: lessons from the Self-Employed Women’s Association (SEWA) (CGAP) https://www.cgap.org/research/publication/confronting-climate-and-health-nexus-lessons-self-employed-womens-association

### Social protection floors

Basic income security that keeps households above the line between one hot season and the next.

Cuts the link: Lost work hours and wages → Informal workers can’t stop work. Who can act: National governments, Development banks, donors and climate funds.

Could help interrupt: The poverty–heat trap

- Guide: Addressing the impacts of extreme heat through social protection (International Labour Organization) https://www.ilo.org/resource/article/addressing-impacts-extreme-heat-through-social-protection

### Free care for heat illness

Covering emergency treatment for heat illness stops one bad day from becoming years of debt.

Cuts the link: Heatstroke and heat exhaustion → Medical costs and debt. Who can act: Health authorities, National governments.

Could help interrupt: The medical-debt trap, The energy-poverty trap

- Guide: Climate change and health: heat-illness guidelines, emergency cooling guidance and heat stroke units (National Centre for Disease Control, India) https://ncdc.mohfw.gov.in/includes/About/CentresAndDivision/CEOH.php

- Guide: National Action Plan on Heat-Related Illness (National Centre for Disease Control, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, India, 2021) https://ncdc.mohfw.gov.in/uploads/pdf/heat12.pdf

### Affordable cooling for the poorest

Lifeline electricity tariffs, efficient fans and cool roofs put safe cooling within reach of every household.

Cuts the link: Can’t afford to keep cool → Heatstroke and heat exhaustion. Who can act: Utilities and energy regulators, City and local governments, National governments.

Could help interrupt: The energy-poverty trap

- Guide: Chilling Prospects: Global Access to Cooling Gaps 2023 (Sustainable Energy for All, 2023) https://www.seforall.org/our-work/research-analysis/chilling-prospects-series/chilling-prospects-global-access-to-cooling-gaps-2023

- Guide: Chilling Prospects Special: Gender and Access to Cooling (Sustainable Energy for All) https://www.seforall.org/our-work/research-analysis/chilling-prospects-series/chilling-prospects-special-gender

### Cool, affordable housing

Upgrading informal settlements with ventilation, shade and cool roofs, and planning homes for people who arrive.

Cuts the link: Forced migration → Homes that trap heat. Who can act: City and local governments, Development banks, donors and climate funds, Community and civil society groups.

Could help interrupt: The displacement loop

In practice: Telangana’s Cool Roof Policy 2023–2028, India’s first, makes cool roofs mandatory for many kinds of building and aims to cover about 300 km² of roofs. Tamil Nadu’s heat strategy proposes making a measure of how much heat walls and roofs let in, the residential envelope transmittance value (ReTV) from India’s residential energy code, a condition in tenders for slum redevelopment.

- Guide: Telangana’s cool roof policy: from pilot demonstration to policy (The Climate Group) https://www.theclimategroup.org/our-work/publications/telanganas-cool-roof-policy-pilot-demonstration-policy-implementation

- Guide: £17.5m for research testing heat adaptations, including a trial of reflective roof coatings with a site in India (Wellcome) https://wellcome.org/insights/articles/wellcome-awards-ps175m-support-global-research-drive

### Keep children in school

Cash transfers, school meals and heat-ready classrooms and timetables keep children learning through hot seasons.

Cuts the link: Deepening inequality → Children pulled out of school. Who can act: Schools and education authorities, National governments.

Could help interrupt: The lost-schooling loop

In practice: When heat closes schools, children lose more than lessons: consultations for Tamil Nadu’s heat strategy found that long breaks cost children in schools serving marginalised groups their midday meals. India’s school meal scheme can keep serving meals through the summer holidays in areas declared drought-hit, as Odisha did in 27 districts in a year when a forecast heatwave also extended school closures. In the Philippines, heat helped drive the return to a June school start, keeping classes out of the hottest months, April and May.

- Guide: Learning Interrupted: global snapshot of climate-related school disruptions (UNICEF, 2026) https://www.unicef.org/reports/learning-interrupted

### Cool nights and support

Cooling centres open at night, shaded and ventilated homes, and mental-health support during the hot season.

Cuts the link: Sleepless hot nights → Mental health suffers. Who can act: City and local governments, Health authorities, Community and civil society groups.

Could help interrupt: The sleepless-nights loop

- Guide: How summer heat affects health, and how to keep cool, including cooling homes at night (WHO Regional Office for Europe, 2025) https://www.who.int/europe/news/item/23-06-2025-how-summer-heat-impacts-health-and-how-to--keepcool

- Guide: Climate and mental health: uncovering how heat affects anxiety, depression and psychosis (Wellcome) https://wellcome.org/research-funding/schemes/climate-and-mental-health-award-uncovering-mechanisms-between-heat-and

### Count every heat death

Real-time tracking of excess deaths during heatwaves, and death certificates that record heat, make the toll visible.

Cuts the link: Heat deaths → Heat deaths under-recorded. Who can act: Health authorities, Weather and climate services, National governments.

Could help interrupt: The invisible-deaths loop

- Guide: Autopsy findings in heat-related deaths: guidance for recording heat as a cause (National Centre for Disease Control, India, in the GHHIN resource library) https://heathealth.info/resources/autopsy-findings-in-heat-related-deaths/

- Guide: National Action Plan on Heat-Related Illness (National Centre for Disease Control, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, India, 2021) https://ncdc.mohfw.gov.in/uploads/pdf/heat12.pdf

### Cooling centres and check-ins

Public cooling spaces, water points and check-ins on older people living alone save lives in every heatwave.

Cuts the link: Heat protection underfunded → Heat deaths. Who can act: City and local governments, Community and civil society groups, Health authorities.

Could help interrupt: The invisible-deaths loop

- Guide: The use of cooling centers to prevent heat-related illness: evidence and strategies for implementation (US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, in the GHHIN resource library) https://heathealth.info/wp-content/uploads/cdc_47657_DS1-compressed-1.pdf

### Dedicated heat budgets

Ring-fenced funding for heat action, set aside before the season, so protection doesn’t compete with the emergency.

Cuts the link: Public budgets strained → Heat protection underfunded. Who can act: National governments, City and local governments, Development banks, donors and climate funds.

Could help interrupt: The reactive-spending loop, The protection-gap loop

In practice: Since August 2026, India’s disaster response funds can pay for heatwave relief; preparing for heat is still paid for separately. In Nepal, Madhesh Province and five municipalities committed 5% of sectoral budgets to adaptation and disaster risk reduction, with support from Practical Action and Mercy Corps.
